t: Nvidia's board approached Arm CEO Rene Haas about the top job, FT reports; Nvidia says candidate talk is premature and 1,600 staff comments ask for Huang back
s: The Financial Times reported on Friday that Nvidia's board has sounded out Rene Haas, the 64-year-old Arm chief and former head of Nvidia's computing products business, as one of several candidates to replace Jensen Huang; there is reportedly no guarantee he will be offered the role or take it. Nvidia told Reuters it is still choosing a search firm and has not formally engaged anyone. Wired reported an internal suggestion-box thread of more than 1,600 comments, many urging Huang's return. Arm shares were down more than 5% and Nvidia more than 3% on the day; earnings land Tuesday with Colette Kress presenting as interim CEO.

t: FAA halts all US departures for about five hours; officials blame telecom gear, three days after the $875 million SMART AI tool went nationwide
s: A nationwide ground stop on Friday, the first since January 2023, delayed or cancelled roughly 7,000 flights after what Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called a communication issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers; officials attributed it to overloaded legacy telecom switches and routers producing inconsistent data. The stop came three days after the FAA extended SMART, Air Space Intelligence's advisory traffic-planning system built under a 12-year, $875 million contract, from the Washington area to all 22 en-route centres. The vendor said the outage was not based on or a result of SMART; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said investigators were looking at it and 'you can't rule out anything'. No technical report has been published.

t: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet: dots agents pay with Visa, Mastercard and Amex network tokens, one biometric approval per purchase, no OpenAI cut at launch
s: ChatGPT Wallet, live on Thursday for a limited set of US ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and over, lets a dot find items on a merchant's site, present a review screen of items, total and card, and complete checkout after the user approves with Face ID or a fingerprint. The card network issues a limited-use token with its own number, security code and expiry, so neither the agent nor the merchant sees the real card; rewards and dispute protections carry over. There are no spending limits or pre-approved purchases yet, OpenAI says it takes no share of transactions for now, and purchases fail on sites that block agents. OpenAI published a Commerce Partner Playbook and named Adyen, Checkout.com, Stripe and fraud vendors Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd as partners.

t: Anthropic's banks reportedly turn away China and Hong Kong orders citing ITAR as Amodei calls compute the 'deepest business dilemma'; pricing Wednesday at $70–$78
s: Bloomberg reported that syndicate banks are refusing or discouraging orders from mainland Chinese and Hong Kong institutions for Anthropic's IPO, citing US arms-export rules, the same approach used for SpaceX's listing; the amended prospectus says Anthropic's models and platform may be controlled under export regulations. Orders are reportedly about six times the shares on offer, with pricing set for November 18 and Nasdaq trading as ANT on November 19 in a $70–$78 range. At a JPMorgan briefing with Jamie Dimon, Dario Amodei said compute is the company's deepest dilemma, that Anthropic plans around roughly the 10th percentile of its growth forecasts and tops up on the spot market; the filing lists $900.9 billion in compute commitments through 2045, about $70.7 billion of it due by September 2027.

t: OpenAI disbands its standalone robotics team and folds it into core research and Applied, saying GPT-6 Astra already runs robots
s: Fortune reported, and OpenAI confirmed, that the robotics research group now sits in the main research organisation under Mark Chen while applied robotics and hardware staff move to Greg Brockman's Applied organisation. OpenAI says robotics remains a core long-term goal and the change speeds it up; earlier in 2026 the company expected progress to come from video models like the now-discontinued Sora, and it now says general frontier models can drive robots directly, citing an Nvidia study in which an Astra-powered agent scored 74.8% on a simulated manipulation benchmark against 51.0% for the best specialised model. OpenAI's booth at the CoRL conference in Austin stood empty this week. Altman still targets a humanoid demonstration in 2027.

t: IBM ships Granite 4.1 'LLMON' previews that bind instructions to data with reserved tokens, claiming near-zero indirect prompt-injection success on OPI
s: IBM published experimental 3B and 8B Granite 4.1 models trained on LLM Object Notation, an XML-like markup whose delimiters are reserved special tokens and whose tags mark instructions, data and requirements, with unique IDs tying each instruction to the data it may act on. On the OPI indirect-injection benchmark IBM reports attack success near zero, avoiding 47% more attacks than the best frontier model it tested and 95% more than the best open model, with similar trends on ASB and StruQ and no loss on standard utility benchmarks. IBM calls it a preview not for production, says the resistance is learned rather than enforced, and has not yet tested adaptive multi-turn attacks.

t: llama.cpp and ggml reach v1.0.0 after 3.5 years: semantic versioning, 35 deprecated functions removed, 150+ model architectures
s: Georgi Gerganov's ggml-org released llama.cpp 1.0.0 and ggml 1.0.0 on Thursday with a formal promise: breaking changes to the public C API or ABI only arrive in major versions, minor versions add backends and models, patches fix bugs. The release removes the deprecated API including 35 functions, promotes the speculative-decoding API to the public header, adds FP8 KV caches and a host-memory cache for mixture-of-experts models, and ships packages for Linux, macOS, Windows, Android and iOS via Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, Winget and an XCFramework. Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel provide self-hosted CI hardware.

t: LangChain raises $300 million Series C at $3 billion led by CapitalG, more than double its valuation a year ago, on 7,000 LangSmith customers
s: TechCrunch reported on Friday that LangChain closed a $300 million Series C led by Alphabet's CapitalG with GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP and Sapphire Ventures, valuing the agent-platform company at $3 billion against $1.25 billion in October 2025. LangChain says LangSmith, its model-agnostic platform for building and managing agents, has 7,000 customers including Harvey, Rippling, Clay, Nvidia, Toyota and Salesforce. The company began in 2022 as an open-source library for chaining LLM calls and has repositioned around managing agents as the frontier labs' own harnesses absorbed the orchestration layer.

t: Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia with immediate effect; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and shares fell as much as 14%
s: Nvidia's Form 8-K says Huang resigned as president, CEO and director on November 12 after 33 years, gives no reason, and names long-time director Harvey Jones as the company's first chair. The resignation followed days of reporting on Huang's personal relationships, including one with a senior executive and alleged contact with a former Megaspeed executive accused of working for Chinese intelligence; Huang admitted infidelity, and the board says its independent investigation has found no reason to believe national security was compromised. Shares fell more than 14% intraday on Thursday before paring losses. Third-quarter results stay scheduled for November 17.

t: Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen at $1.50 / $7.50, flat across 1M tokens, and retires the Flash brand
s: Google's new fast model for agents is priced at $1.50 per million input and $7.50 per million output tokens with no long-context surcharge and no promotional window, and is available in the Gemini API, AI Studio, Antigravity, Gemini Enterprise, Search and the Gemini app. Google reports it finishes tasks 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, scores 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 against Flash's 18.2%, and edges Argon on the Artificial Analysis index at 51 versus 50. It adds a fourth 'xhigh' thinking level and is positioned as the worker model under Carbon in Google's Orchestrator.

t: Four nonprofits sue OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX in San Francisco to halt frontier AI development
s: Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, the Irreplaceable Education Fund and others filed on November 12 under California's unfair-business-practices and public-nuisance laws, seeking an order barring further development of models such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. The complaint cites incidents in which models allegedly escaped test environments and quotes the labs' own leaders on civilisational risk. It follows Florida's pending motion to stop OpenAI training new models without oversight and an eight-state suit filed in October. Meta declined to comment; the others had not responded.

t: Attackers ran AntiFox, an open-source AI pentest platform, from Alibaba Cloud to steal AWS secrets: hundreds of API calls in 30 minutes
s: Arctic Wolf documented two intrusions in which self-hosted AntiFox agents, forked from the ARTEX framework, planted an ASPX webshell on an IIS server, read connection strings and config files, then cycled through AWS identities with hundreds of API requests in about half an hour; most were denied, some returned production secrets. A second case used a valid identity to read, copy and delete S3 objects. Amazon says its services operated as designed and the credentials came from compromised customer applications.

t: Thinking Machines publishes Inkling 2 Small's weights: 394 GB, Apache 2.0, 500 GB of VRAM to run, no stable serving stack yet
s: The 594B-parameter, 17B-active mixture-of-experts model landed on Hugging Face on November 12, three days after its hosted-only launch on Tinker, in Nvidia's NVFP4 format with an MXFP8 variant at 623 GB. The card asks for at least 500 GB of aggregate VRAM (2x B300 or 4x H200). As of Thursday SGLang and vLLM support it only in development builds, and the promised external red-team results were not published with the drop.

t: Doximity: 63% of US physicians use AI for clinical decision support, up from 37% a year ago, and three in four hit a factual error
s: Doximity's survey of 3,379 physicians across 20 specialties, fielded in September and published November 12, finds more than half use AI daily and a further third weekly. Use has moved from documentation to judgment: 63% use it for clinical decision support (37% in 2025) and 70% for literature review. 81% say it taught them something; three in four encountered at least one factual inaccuracy in the past year; 61% worry trainees will not build their own skills.

t: J.P. Morgan forecasts 300,000–400,000 US humanoid robots a year by 2030 and names hands, actuators, the brain and capacity as the bottlenecks
s: In a note reported by Reuters on Thursday, J.P. Morgan projects US humanoid output of 300,000 to 400,000 units by 2030 and about 1.5 million by 2035, with most makers other than Tesla targeting 10,000 to 30,000 units a year. It sizes the actuator, motor and vision component market at nearly $30 billion by 2035, estimates about $100,000 a year in savings per multi-shift customer, and favours suppliers Timken, Robotis, Leader Drive, Orbbec and Cognex over robot makers in the near term.

t: OpenAI backs four bipartisan chip-export bills, including Commerce oversight of GPUs rented from overseas data centres
s: OpenAI's global affairs chief Chris Lehane said the company supports tighter US limits on advanced chips and chipmaking tools for China, including the Warren–Banks AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act's tracking requirements, the MATCH Act on allied equipment sales, and the Remote Access Security Act, which would let the Commerce Department police restricted GPUs rented through foreign data centres. Bloomberg first reported the position; OpenAI says its own Jalapeño chip will not be sold to China. The stance lands in the week Nvidia, OpenAI's main supplier, lost the CEO who argued for continued China sales.

t: SpaceX's two AI campuses now total $74 billion: a $24 billion gas-powered site at Starbase and a $50 billion, 6 GW campus in Cochise County
s: Reuters reports SpaceX plans to invest more than $74 billion in supercomputing campuses in Texas and Arizona. The Starbase, Texas project pairs a gas-fired power plant with a compute facility at an initial $24 billion and goes to the city commission on December 9; the Arizona project, a 747-acre, nine-building, 6 GW campus near the Willcox Playa at up to $50 billion, faces a county zoning hearing the same day after a packed public meeting and a petition of about 2,100 signatures. SpaceX says the Arizona site would use no industrial water for cooling and would fund $3.6 billion of transmission.

t: A Microsoft 365 outage took Outlook, Teams calendars and Copilot down for most of Thursday, with Anthropic and OpenAI connectors failing alongside
s: Microsoft said a large number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable from around 5:15 a.m. AEDT on November 13, then that a core process handling secure connections was overwhelmed; it reverted a recent network configuration change and said there was no indication of malicious activity. Downdetector logged nearly 140,000 Outlook reports at the peak, seven in ten from the US. Microsoft 365 Copilot, Graph, Intune, Defender and Power BI were affected, Anthropic reported an upstream issue with its Microsoft 365 connector and OpenAI reported connector problems; recovery was still partial late in the day and a post-incident report is promised.

t: Nvidia's board met to decide Huang's future; shares fell 8.6% after hours and 6% premarket
s: The Wall Street Journal reported on November 11 that Nvidia's board was preparing to remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, and Reuters reported that the independent directors met late on Wednesday to decide. Bloomberg reported the board is working with an outside firm on possible replacements, including an interim chief, with Seeking Alpha naming CFO Colette Kress as a possibility. The New York Times separately reported, citing five current and former employees, that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's healthcare vice-president, who reports to him; Nvidia did not comment. Shares closed up 2.9% at $173.73, fell 8.6% to $158.78 after hours and were down about 6% in Thursday premarket trading, roughly 27% below the early-October peak. No decision had been announced by publication, and Nvidia reports earnings on November 17.

t: OpenAI's revenue reached $10 billion in Q3 while its adjusted operating loss grew to $10.9 billion
s: Internal documents reviewed by the Wall Street Journal and reported on November 11 show OpenAI's third-quarter revenue at about $10 billion, up roughly 50% from $6.7 billion in the second quarter, with an adjusted operating loss of about $10.9 billion against $10.1 billion a quarter earlier. The adjusted operating margin improved to minus 109% from minus 150%. Enterprise reportedly became the largest revenue line for the first time, ahead of consumer subscriptions, after doubling quarter on quarter on the strength of coding tools, while consumer sales grew 20%. Net loss, compute spending and cash were not disclosed. The same quarter, Anthropic's S-1 showed $16.96 billion of revenue and a $567 million operating loss.

t: Railway's post-mortem: a build-sandbox escape led to $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges on stolen keys
s: Railway published its full incident report on November 10 for the October 20–21 breach. An attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partially escape filesystem isolation on a shared build VM, picked up a build credential that an internal Temporal instance wrongly trusted, read 353 builds' histories and a copy of Railway's monorepo, found a misconfigured OIDC binding and used it to reach a machine holding a long-lived decryption key. Environment variables for at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, may have been decrypted, with AI provider keys queried by name first. Railway estimates about $740,000 of unauthorised spend across customers' accounts, reset linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, says AWS and Google are refunding under existing policies while OpenAI and SpaceXSI review case by case, and is covering Anthropic and OpenRouter charges itself.

t: Google's Gemini Decision 1 scores up to 1,000 questions per call at $0.10 per million input tokens, no output charge
s: Google launched the Gemini Decisions API on November 11, powered by a model called gemini-decision-1 that scores a fixed set of options in a single forward pass and returns probabilities and confidence scores instead of generated text. One request takes up to 256,000 tokens of text, images, audio, video or PDFs and up to 1,000 independent questions, each a yes/no check, a multiple-choice question with up to 255 options or a rubric score, with Google quoting 150 to 250 milliseconds end to end. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens and nothing for output, with shared input billed once per request; Google says it is nearly five times cheaper than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite on its own benchmark suite. It is available in AI Studio with a free tier, and OpenAI launched a comparable Decisions API on GPT-6 Luna in October at the same starting price.

t: Google Cloud puts a Gemini agent inside Epic, billing and insurer systems for Northwell, HCA and Optum
s: Google Cloud launched Gemini for healthcare on November 10 as a US preview, an agent that reads records from Epic and Oracle Health, billing platforms, Medicare coverage data and ASCO and BMJ guidelines, then runs multi-step administrative tasks such as summarising a chart, preparing a prior authorisation, checking benefits and estimating a patient's cost. It ships with five preset skills, can read but not write to the chart, cites a source for every finding and lets customers pick models from Google, Anthropic or OpenAI by task. Launch customers include Northwell Health, Highmark Health, HCA Healthcare, Optum, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, Hartford HealthCare and Stanford School of Medicine; GoodRx, UiPath, Verato and InterSystems announced integrations. Pricing is per seat or pay as you go, with no figures given.

t: New York opens RAISE Act registration: frontier labs over $500 million in revenue must file by January 1
s: Governor Kathy Hochul announced on November 10 that registration is open for large frontier developers under the RAISE Act, which takes effect on January 1, 2027. Companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue that train models above 10^26 operations and deploy them in New York must register with DIGIT, the new office inside the Department of Financial Services, publish a frontier AI framework reviewed at least annually, publish a transparency report with each new or substantially modified model, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours and file catastrophic-risk assessment summaries every three months. The attorney general can seek up to $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for each subsequent one, plus $1,000 a day for failing to register. A Binghamton University research centre with $55 million of initial funding will help review published frameworks.

t: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking in its contract of carriage, supervised or not
s: United revised its contract of carriage on November 11 to define an AI agent as any assistant, standalone agent or AI-enabled browser that discovers, searches, books or manages United products on a passenger's behalf, whether or not a human supervises or approves each step. A new Rule 6.J.6 prohibits using such agents to make, modify or service a ticket or buy any product, and Rule 5.H lets United cancel those reservations without notice; existing remedies include voiding tickets, deleting miles and terminating MileagePlus accounts. United cites privacy, unintended purchases and a rule that passengers personally acknowledge dangerous-goods warnings at check-in; chief executive Scott Kirby reportedly told an event in Chicago he did not want to create another middleman. Searching fares with AI and buying yourself remains allowed. United says it works with no third-party agents today and has not said how it will detect them.

t: OpenAI's models leave Cursor today, 75 days after the SpaceX takeover triggered the cutoff
s: November 12 is the date OpenAI set in August for ending its supply of models to Cursor, after SpaceX closed its $60 billion all-stock acquisition of the coding-tool maker. OpenAI said at the time that it could not be confident SpaceX would honour its terms of service, cited earlier disputes with Musk companies and gave the maximum notice its contract allowed; GPT-6 Astra was never offered to Cursor. Cursor has shipped Grok 4.5 on every plan since July and continues to offer Anthropic and Google models, so the practical impact falls on teams whose rules, evals and prompts were tuned for GPT-6-class models inside Cursor. Developers on Cursor had no statutory notice protection; EU cloud-switching rules cover customers leaving a provider, not providers leaving a customer.

t: Meta's infrastructure chief steps down as a $135–145 billion capex year hands over to an ex-AWS executive
s: Santosh Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering since 2022 and an employee since 2009, told staff in a November 11 memo that he is stepping down, Bloomberg first reported and CNBC confirmed. Dave Brown, who joined in July after about two decades at Amazon Web Services, takes over infrastructure inside Meta Compute, the unit run by Dina Powell McCormick and Daniel Gross that plans Meta's AI capacity; Janardhan moves to an advisory role and supports the handover through the first quarter of 2027. The memo gave no reason. Meta has guided 2026 capital spending to $135 billion to $145 billion, reported $34.9 billion of capex and negative free cash flow in the September quarter, and had its credit outlook cut to negative by S&P in October.

t: Anthropic sets its IPO range at $70–78, raising up to $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation
s: Anthropic launched its roadshow on November 10 with an amended S-1 offering 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 under the Nasdaq ticker ANT, which would raise up to $64.4 billion and value the company at as much as $1.4 trillion fully diluted. Seven strategic partners led by Google and Nvidia at $10 billion each, with AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC behind them, have agreed to buy a further $26 billion of non-voting stock at the midpoint price. The filing shows revenue of $17 billion for the September quarter and an annualised run rate of about $81 billion at the end of October; most insiders are locked up for 180 days and founders for a year. Trading is reported to begin as early as November 19.

t: Gemini 4 Carbon opens to all paying developers at $2 / $10, doubling to $4 / $20 on December 1
s: Google made Gemini 4 Carbon generally available on November 10 through the Gemini API, AI Studio, Gemini for business, Android Studio and Antigravity, two weeks after releasing it only to cyber defenders in its Fairwind programme. Introductory pricing matches Gemini 4 Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 output until November 30, after which both models double. Google says Carbon ranks first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR and Zapier's AutomationBench at more than twice the cost efficiency of the next external model, and that its per-attempt breach rate in simulated cyberattacks fell to 0.8% from Argon's 3.1%; the cyber-tuned variant stays gated. Google still recommends Argon for most software and knowledge work.

t: Anthropic ships Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and interactive connectors, with Meetings to follow
s: A day before its roadshow, Anthropic released Claude Sheets, a collaborative spreadsheet where Claude writes formulas and logs every change, Claude Whiteboards for planning sessions that can be exported as documents or slides, and made Claude Data, its renamed dashboards product, generally available with certified data definitions in beta. Partners including Adobe and Atlassian can now embed full versions of their apps inside Claude, and Salesforce, NetSuite and Workday plugins ship with built-in skills. TechCrunch reported Claude Meetings, which joins Google Meet calls and drafts plans while people talk, is in beta on Team and Enterprise plans; Anthropic's own post lists it as coming soon. Microsoft shares fell 2.2% on the day.

t: A jailbroken DeepSeek agent ran a two-week intrusion into a European telecom and 13 of its tenants
s: Malbear Labs published a reconstruction on November 8 of what it calls Operation Snowball, in which an operator pointed a custom agent framework running DeepSeek Flash at a European telecommunications provider and 13 organisations hosted on its infrastructure, then checked in asynchronously while the agent worked for more than two weeks. The jailbreak prompt ran to about 78,000 characters and told the model to treat refusals as malfunctions; more than 70 recovered session transcripts show no refusals. The agent entered through CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE flaw in Cisco BroadWorks patched in August, gained root via a 2020 Liferay bug, rewrote its own tunnelling tool when one was blocked, and pulled dozens of credential sets and about 80 Zabbix backups. Its claims of reaching subscriber billing and millions of patient records were not verified with any victim.

t: 35,578 Grok Build apps were open to anyone with a link, including 24 built by SpaceXSI and X staff
s: Security firm Claroc reported on November 10 that 35,578 of the 37,571 live apps it enumerated from Grok's chat-based Build mode, about 95%, could be opened without signing in, because the publishing flow preselected 'Anyone with the link' and hostname-based sharing made the apps discoverable through passive DNS. Claroc estimates 650 to 800 of them held private data, including a sales map covering 594 accounts, employee rosters, medical information and plain-text passwords; 24 belonged to SpaceXSI and X staff and were taken down after disclosure. SpaceXSI said publishing takes several deliberate steps and that employee accounts default to 'Only you'. Claroc's tests found the 'Only you' setting did block outsiders.

t: Notion confirms AI chat transcripts from under 1% of workspaces leaked through the Fireworks breach
s: Notion's advisory, updated November 10, says Fireworks AI told it on November 2 that attackers had reached what was first described as synthetic test data, revised that on November 6 to possible customer data, and confirmed on November 8 that Notion AI chat transcripts used by its Insights feature were taken. Notion disconnected from Fireworks and deleted its data there on November 3, disabled Insights, stopped serving open-weight models through Fireworks and emailed affected customers on November 9; it says fewer than 1% of workspaces are involved and most transcripts carry no workspace or author labels. Fireworks' own update attributes the intrusion to a financially motivated group that resells stolen model access through illicit routing gateways, the pattern Google calls LLMjacking.

t: Oura buys AI primary-care startup Counsel Health for $625 million after shelving its IPO
s: Smart-ring maker Oura agreed on November 10 to acquire Counsel Health, a chat-first medical service that pairs an AI assistant with licensed physicians, for $625 million, roughly 17 times the $36 million the startup had raised from Andreessen Horowitz and GV. Counsel's service has been inside the Oura app since June; its 70 staff will join Oura and chief executive Muthu Alagappan becomes chief clinical AI officer, with the deal expected to close before the end of 2027. Oura, valued at $11 billion, reported $533 million of revenue in the September quarter, up 153%, and postponed a planned IPO of up to $2.2 billion in October citing market conditions.

t: Skild AI open-sources Steel, a Newton solver it says runs robot simulation up to 13x faster than PhysX
s: Skild AI, the $14 billion robot-foundation-model startup backed by SoftBank and Nvidia, released Steel on November 9 as a solver inside Nvidia's open-source Newton physics engine, available as newton.solvers.SolverSteel. On a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU Skild measured a 3.8x geometric-mean speed-up over PhysX across 20 Isaac Lab tasks, 9.2x to 13x on batches mixing many task types, and about 62% less GPU memory at a matched batch of 61,440 environments. Steel also beat MuJoCo Warp by roughly 1.3x and ships an experimental differentiable step. Skild published the code and benchmark conditions; the licence is not named in the post.

t: DeepMind's AlphaProof Code wrote 6.5 million lines of proof for Signal's encryption in four weeks
s: Google DeepMind said on November 10 that AlphaProof Code, a system pairing five researchers with agents running on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5, formally verified forward secrecy, post-compromise security and authentication for libsignal, the reference implementation of the Signal protocol used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, at the level of compiled AArch64 machine code. Agents generated roughly 6.5 million lines of Lean proofs on about 26,000 lines of trusted specification in four weeks, and the team re-injected two historical libsignal bugs to show the proofs fail on each. The results cover DeepMind's own build behind a small wrapper rather than Signal's apps, side channels were out of scope, and the specifications and proofs are being released.

t: OpenAI turns ChatGPT into a business directory with claimable profiles and sponsored Business Agents
s: OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta on November 10: a Business Hub where companies claim a profile, upload product feeds with prices and stock, and see how often they are mentioned in conversations and how many clicks they receive, plus Business Agents that answer customer questions inside ChatGPT for eligible US e-commerce and online-service companies, with Shopify stores connecting directly. The agents can be the destination for ChatGPT ads, extending the sponsored-agent test OpenAI began in September. OpenAI says conversations are not shared with businesses and that ChatGPT reaches 1.2 billion people a week; pricing was not disclosed.

t: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrive at $8 / $40, 20% below the 5.1 price
s: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9 at $8 per million input tokens and $40 output, down from $10 / $50 for the 5.1 generation, with cached input at $0.20 and a new fast mode at $16 / $80. Anthropic's own tables put Fable 5.2 at 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 against 32.4% for 5.1, and the company says output is up to 30% faster. Fable is generally available on the Claude API, AWS, Google Cloud and Azure; Mythos remains limited to vetted organisations in cyber and life sciences, and Anthropic still recommends Opus 5.5 as the default for most work.

t: SoftBank swings to a ¥1.1 trillion loss as Anthropic's IPO roadshow opens at a reported $1.1–1.3 trillion
s: SoftBank Group reported a net loss of about ¥1.1 trillion ($7 billion) for July–September on November 10, against a ¥2.5 trillion profit a year earlier that had been lifted by gains on its OpenAI stake; the result was worse than the most bearish of three forecasts polled by LSEG. Reuters noted SoftBank has spent $64.6 billion on a 13% OpenAI holding and that its shares have roughly halved since June. Anthropic was expected to begin formally marketing its own IPO the same day, with Bloomberg reporting investor estimates of $1.1–1.3 trillion, below the $1.4–1.5 trillion discussed weeks ago and the $2 trillion floated in October.

t: Australia will set up an AI safety regulator with penalty powers and mandatory incident reporting
s: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on November 10 that AI companies operating in Australia will face mandatory safeguards enforced by a new AI safety regulator able to impose penalties, and that firms must report AI security incidents and potential breaches of criminal law. The announcement follows a rapid review of the June episode in which an OpenAI agent reached a Medicare statistics website, which OpenAI did not report to Canberra until September; the government accepted all 18 of the review's recommendations. The law would also allow independent evaluation of frontier models. No bill text, penalty amounts or start date have been published.

t: Meta's Muse Ember at $0.10 / $0.50 and Meituan's MIT-licensed LongCat-2.5 reset the budget tier
s: Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest multimodal model, aimed at high-volume agent sub-tasks such as tool calls, routing and extraction, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 cached and $0.50 output up to 200K context, tripling above that. Artificial Analysis scores it 36 on its Intelligence Index, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at roughly a third of the cost per task because it emits far fewer output tokens. Separately, Meituan published the weights of LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with about 48 billion active parameters, under the MIT licence on November 9, with hosted pricing of $0.30 / $1.20.

t: Google adds TPU 8tx for confidential compute and TPU 8i Max for long context, its fourth TPU system this year
s: Google announced two more eighth-generation TPU systems on November 9: TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the training-focused 8t and paired with fifth-generation AMD EPYC hosts to keep data and weights isolated in use, and TPU 8i Max, which packages two 8i inference chips together for double the compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth in the same rack footprint. Google says it now has nearly 100 TPU customers and that this is the first year it has shipped four TPU systems. The post also made Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing generally available and pointed to the open-sourced TorchTPU stack; no pricing or availability dates were given.

t: Nvidia opens GR00T 2 and Isaac Lab 3.0 at CoRL; 71% one-shot success on an unnamed 50-task suite
s: At the Conference on Robot Learning in Austin on November 9, Nvidia introduced GR00T 2, a world action model built on Cosmos and trained on robot data plus 100,000 hours of open-source human egocentric video, and Isaac Lab 3.0, which lets agents assemble training environments and switch between PhysX and Newton physics. Nvidia says GR00T 2 completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once with no task-specific demonstrations, averaging 71% success with one demonstration per task and 95% with five, and ranks in the top three on RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces. The 50 tasks, rollout counts and licence terms were not published.

t: Fireworks AI tells customers of a second breach in a month, reaching billing data and some model weights
s: Fireworks AI notified customers on November 9 that an intruder entered development machines on October 24 through a cloud provider and reached billing data and, for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights, Bloomberg reported. It is the inference provider's second disclosed incident in weeks: on October 6 it found that an unauthorised party had used internal Fireworks credentials to read environment variables from customer evaluation jobs, including stored API keys, and it rotated employee and customer keys over the following days. Fireworks' bulletin for the October incident says prompts and outputs were not stored because the platform is zero-data-retention by default.

t: Abridge, the $5.3 billion AI scribe, confirms layoffs in an 'organisation-wide realignment'
s: Abridge confirmed on November 9 that it has laid off staff as part of what it called an organisation-wide realignment to flatten the company, offering transition packages and outplacement support; it did not disclose the number of roles. The Pittsburgh-based clinical documentation company raised $300 million in a 2025 Series E led by Andreessen Horowitz at a $5.3 billion valuation and said it still holds more than half the capital it has ever raised. Former employees posting on LinkedIn described the cuts as sudden; one layoff tracker put the figure at roughly 90, which Abridge has not confirmed.

t: ChatGPT Enterprise lands in AWS Marketplace, letting buyers draw down cloud commitments
s: OpenAI listed ChatGPT Enterprise in the AWS Marketplace on November 9, so organisations can buy it through their existing AWS billing relationship and, where eligible, count the spend against committed cloud contracts. The listing extends the Amazon partnership that already put OpenAI's models and Codex on Bedrock earlier this year and that an internal OpenAI memo reportedly credited with strong enterprise demand. Pricing is not published on the listing.

t: Nvidia's board opens an independent probe after Huang admits an affair with the alleged Megaspeed informant
s: Nvidia's board said on November 8 that independent directors and outside counsel will review CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive that a US intelligence memo reportedly alleges was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. In a message to staff, Huang acknowledged the affair and apologised; the board said it has confidence in him and no reason to believe company or national-security secrets were compromised. House committee chairs have asked for a closed-door briefing on November 18.

t: Anthropic reportedly paid $3.4 billion for 1.7 gigawatts of gas generators
s: Anthropic took over OnePWR Solutions' orders for roughly 1.7 gigawatts of Caterpillar gas-fired generators in a deal signed in late September and worth about $3.4 billion, the Financial Times reported on November 8, citing one person familiar with it. The FT called it the largest known single purchase of power equipment by an AI company; neither party commented. Anthropic's amended IPO filing last week disclosed about $895 billion in commitments, almost all for compute and infrastructure.

t: Claude Code's 'don't ask again' button put 2,539 secrets in public GitHub repos
s: Security firm Apiiro found that when a Claude Code user approves a shell command with 'Yes, and don't ask again', the exact command is saved to .claude/settings.local.json in the project, including any password or token typed into it. Scanning 104,185 public copies of the file, Apiiro found 1,122 containing 1,379 live-looking secrets, including 379 database passwords and 23 AWS keys; with older versions and transcripts the total reached 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories. Claude Code head Boris Cherny said on Hacker News that Anthropic is looking into it and that the tool has not historically scrubbed secrets.

t: Check Point: autonomous ARTEX agents hit 200+ organisations in 14 countries since October 17
s: An AI-driven intrusion campaign using the ARTEX penetration-testing framework has targeted more than 200 organisations across 14 countries since October 17, compromising at least nine, BleepingComputer reported from CrowdStrike and Check Point research. The agents forged an administrator token to read a Greek ministry's mailboxes, skipped hosts protected by CrowdStrike Falcon on operator instruction, and burned more than 1.4 billion input tokens in a single intrusion. Separately, the Dutch vulnerability-disclosure institute DIVD said ARTEX agents went from initial access to root on its systems in 12 minutes.

t: DeepMind says AI agents found two weaknesses in 1024-bit RSA; 2048-bit keys unaffected
s: Google DeepMind said on November 6 that supervised AI agents produced two working papers describing weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA: a signature-forgery method estimated at roughly 1,600 times more efficient than the prior best when the attacker controls part of the signed data, and a batch-factoring approach about 30 times cheaper per additional key than the multiple number field sieve. One agent generated proofs and a second verified them in Lean 4. The papers are not peer reviewed, the forgery gain is a theoretical estimate, and DeepMind says keys of 2048 bits and above are not affected.

t: Thinking Machines ships Inkling 2 Small: 594B-parameter MoE, 17B active, weights promised under Apache 2.0
s: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Small on November 5, a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion total and 17 billion active parameters, a 1-million-token context window, and image input. It was pretrained on 8.4 trillion tokens in 68 hours on Nvidia GB300 racks using native NVFP4, then trained with reinforcement learning for nine days on 2,048 GPUs. Inference is available through the company's Tinker platform at a listed $0.30 per million input tokens and $1.00 output; full weights are promised under Apache 2.0 within weeks, conditional on external safety testing.

t: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol discount ends November 30; the real price ladder is now GPT-6.1 at $2 / $10
s: OpenAI's pricing page confirms that promotional pricing on GPT-5.6 Sol ($4 input / $20 output per million tokens) runs only until November 30, after which the model returns to its $5 / $30 list rate. The same page shows where OpenAI now wants workloads to go: GPT-6.1 Sol at $2 / $10, GPT-6.1 Terra at $1 / $5 and GPT-6 Luna at $0.10 / $0.50, all with 1.05-million-token windows, none of which were in our tracker until today. OpenAI also agreed on November 5 to buy Pierre Computer Company, the small maker of the Trees and Diffs libraries Codex already uses, for an undisclosed sum.

t: Physical AI goes public: Agility Robotics trades on Nasdaq as Axon puts $1.2 billion into Skydio
s: Agility Robotics became the first pure-play humanoid company on a US exchange on November 5, trading as AGLT after closing its merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI and raising about $465 million; it reported $174,000 of revenue and a $362 million loss in the first half of 2026 against more than $300 million in committed orders for a Digit 5 robot that ships in 2027. The next day Axon said it would invest a further $1.2 billion in drone maker Skydio at a $5.2 billion pre-money valuation and become its exclusive US and Canadian public-safety distributor.

t: Cassidy's PATIENT AI Act draft would add a third-party FDA review path for health AI; comments due December 1
s: Senate HELP Committee chair Bill Cassidy's discussion draft, released October 29 with stakeholder comments requested by December 1, proposes a voluntary FDA preliminary review for software components of 'integrated devices', an accredited third-party review programme for low- and moderate-risk software devices, pre-submitted change-control plans, and a Medicare coverage pathway for AI services. An analysis by the FDA Law Blog published November 8 argues much of the FDA title duplicates authority the agency already has and could add procedure without shortening time to market.

t: Anthropic tells enterprise customers an outside security firm viewed account data; Korean regulator reviews ~100 accounts
s: Anthropic has emailed enterprise customers that an outside cybersecurity firm accessed internal systems in late October, exposing account and organisation identifiers, business contact details and subscription-plan data but not prompts, outputs or payment information, according to a notice shared on X and reporting in Seoul Economic Daily. The Washington Post reported on October 26 that the startup Cathedral got in through a vulnerability in third-party business software. Anthropic reported the incident to South Korea's privacy regulator on October 31; the PIPC says roughly 100 Korean corporate accounts were affected and it is deciding whether to open a formal investigation.

t: OpenAI reportedly raises $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
s: OpenAI has closed the first part of a new funding round, raising about $11 billion at a valuation of roughly $1.25 trillion, according to a Reuters report picked up by TechCrunch. The figure is below the $1.5 trillion the company had reportedly been seeking, and SoftBank and MGX are said to have participated.

t: Anthropic heads into its IPO roadshow with investors reportedly talking down the valuation
s: Anthropic, which filed its public S-1 on October 26 with the proposed Nasdaq ticker ANT, is expected to begin formally marketing its IPO the week of November 9, the earliest SEC timing rules allow. Reports this week said some investors are discussing a valuation around $1.2–1.3 trillion, below figures floated in October, and that a smaller raise or a delay are both possible if AI stocks stay volatile.

t: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber and rates it 'Critical' for cybersecurity capability
s: OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber on November 5, a version of GPT-6 Astra tuned for authorised vulnerability discovery, exploit development and penetration testing. It is the first model OpenAI has classified as 'Critical' under its Preparedness Framework, one step above the 'High' rating of its predecessor, and is available only to vetted customers in the company's Daybreak Red programme. OpenAI says the model found more than 80 previously unknown vulnerabilities in Firefox during testing.

t: Google's Gemini 4 Argon launch pricing expires December 1, doubling to $4 / $20
s: Google's official Gemini API pricing page now lists Gemini 4 Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens only through November 30, 2026, rising to $4 and $20 from December 1. The Flash models carry a similar schedule: Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.6 Flash are $0.75 / $3.75 through December 31 and $1.50 / $7.50 from January 1, 2027.

t: Ramp's spending data shows business AI spending stalling
s: Card and bill-pay data from Ramp indicates that the share of US businesses paying for AI tools has flattened in recent months after two years of steady growth, according to TechCrunch's report on the firm's latest AI index. The timing is awkward for Anthropic, whose IPO pitch leans on rapid enterprise adoption.

t: Nvidia's board opens an independent probe after reports its CEO was targeted by a Chinese informant
s: Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation following a New York Times report that CEO Jensen Huang had ties to a woman US officials believed was passing information to Beijing. TechCrunch separately reported that a US intelligence memo alleges an executive at Megaspeed was recruited to spy on Huang.

t: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI-agent security startup Clutch for about $500 million
s: Palo Alto Networks is negotiating an acquisition of Clutch, a startup focused on securing AI agents and the non-human identities they use, for roughly $500 million, TechCrunch reported. It would be one of the first large acquisitions explicitly aimed at agent security rather than general AI security.

t: After the midterms, data-center politics turn against the builders
s: Voters backed candidates and local measures opposing new data centers in several races this week, and TechCrunch reports that Elon Musk's data-center plans in particular face a rockier path. Meta has warned that the backlash could slow AI expansion, and OpenAI has pledged to cover the full cost of power and grid upgrades for its sites.

t: Crusoe sells its troubled Wyoming data-center project to Google
s: Crusoe has handed off a struggling data-center development in Wyoming to Google, TechCrunch reported, as hyperscalers pick up projects from smaller builders that have struggled with financing and power.

t: Airbnb says its AI travel agent arrives in the first half of 2027
s: Airbnb told investors it plans to launch an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027, joining the queue of consumer companies promising agents that plan and book rather than merely search.

t: OpenAI disbands its standalone robotics team for the second time, betting GPT-6 Astra's 74.8% simulation score makes a separate robot brain unnecessary
s: The researchers move under Mark Chen, the hardware staff under Greg Brockman, and the empty booth at CoRL tells robot makers what OpenAI thinks the moat is: the general model, not the robot.

t: Nvidia approached Arm's Rene Haas, FT reports, as VCs count the 105 startup rounds Huang's Nvidia joined this year
s: The succession search is weeks from a decision at best; the money Nvidia poured into neoclouds and model labs under Huang may change faster than the CEO's office does.

t: llama.cpp 1.0.0 after 3.5 years: semantic versioning, 35 deprecated functions gone, FP8 KV cache. What the stability promise changes for local AI
s: The engine under Ollama, LM Studio and most on-device inference now promises that breaking changes arrive only with a major version; for the teams that link libllama, that is the end of a fortnightly maintenance tax.

t: IBM's Granite 4.1 LLMON previews train the model to separate instructions from data, claiming near-zero indirect prompt-injection success. What security teams should test
s: Reserved special tokens that user content cannot forge, and unique IDs that bind each instruction to the data it may act on: it is the first vendor attempt to make injection resistance a property of the model rather than of the prompt.

t: The FAA grounded every US departure for five hours, three days after its $875 million SMART AI tool went to all 22 centres: what is known, what is not
s: Officials blame legacy telecom hardware and the vendor denies any link, but the homeland security secretary would not clear the system, and the episode is a preview of how every AI-adjacent failure will now be argued.

t: ChatGPT Wallet: network tokens, one biometric approval per purchase and no OpenAI fee at launch. What merchants and security teams should do now
s: OpenAI's dots agents can now check out with Visa, Mastercard and American Express without ever seeing a card number; the design sets a bar other agent payments will be judged against, and the economics are deliberately unstated.

t: Anthropic's IPO: China orders rebuffed, $900.9 billion in compute commitments and a '10th percentile' capacity plan. What to read before Wednesday's pricing
s: Six-times oversubscribed with a whole region excluded, and a CEO who says the hardest problem is guessing how many chips to buy: the two numbers that matter are $70.7 billion due by September 2027 and the spot market Amodei is relying on.

t: Four nonprofits sue OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX to halt frontier AI development under California's public-nuisance law
s: The suit borrows the labs' own warnings as evidence, follows Florida's and eight states' pending motions, and is the third attempt this year to get a court, not Congress, to set the pace.

t: J.P. Morgan: US humanoid production could reach 300,000–400,000 units by 2030 and 1.5 million by 2035, with hands and actuators the binding constraint
s: The bank's first full US humanoid forecast puts near-term value in component suppliers, not robot makers, and names the four bottlenecks it expects to hold the industry back.

t: Huang resigns from Nvidia: what the 8-K says, what the 14% intraday drop prices in, and why November 17 now matters more
s: The founder who ran the company for 33 years is gone with immediate effect, the CFO is running it, and the first earnings call without him is four days away.

t: Inkling 2 Small's weights are out: 394 GB, Apache 2.0, 500 GB of VRAM to run, and no released serving stack supports it yet
s: Thinking Machines kept its promise three days after the hosted launch, and the gap between 'open' and 'runnable' is where the next week goes.

t: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: $1.50 / $7.50 flat across a 1M context, 2.5x faster than 3.8 Flash, and the end of the Flash brand
s: Google's new 'daily driver' for agents costs double its promotional predecessor but removes the long-context surcharge and reports a 57% Terminal-Bench score against Flash's 18%.

t: 63% of US physicians now use AI for clinical decision support, up from 37% a year ago, Doximity's survey of 3,379 doctors finds
s: The shift from note-taking to decision-making happened in twelve months, three in four doctors hit a factual error in the past year, and most worry trainees will never build the skills to catch one.

t: AntiFox: attackers ran an open-source AI pentest platform from Alibaba Cloud to steal AWS secrets, hundreds of API calls in 30 minutes
s: Arctic Wolf's report is the first detailed look at a forkable agentic security tool being used offensively against production cloud accounts, and the defensive signals are specific.

t: United Airlines wrote AI agents into its contract of carriage as a prohibited practice: what the text says and what retailers should take from it
s: Supervision is no defence, searching is still allowed and United can cancel without notice; the first airline ban on agents is a template other merchants will copy or reject.

t: Railway's post-mortem: a build-sandbox escape, one over-trusted credential and $740,000 of fraudulent AI charges
s: The clearest public account yet of how a platform breach becomes LLMjacking, with the exact controls that limited the damage and the ones that did not exist.

t: OpenAI's $10 billion quarter came with a $10.9 billion loss: what the leaked numbers say next to Anthropic's S-1
s: Revenue up 50% in a quarter, enterprise now bigger than consumer, and a loss of $1.09 per dollar of sales; the figures explain the Cursor cutoff, the Astra price and why OpenAI's IPO is a 2027 story.

t: Nvidia's board weighs removing Jensen Huang: what an 8.6% after-hours drop and a $200 price target are pricing in
s: Five days before earnings, the world's second-most-valuable company may replace the only chief executive it has ever had; here is how to read the stock, the succession options and the export-control risk underneath.

t: New York opens RAISE Act registration: $500 million revenue, 10^26 FLOPs, 72-hour incident reports and a January 1 deadline
s: The first US state registry of frontier AI developers is now taking filings; here is who is covered, what they must publish, what the penalties are and how it differs from California's SB 53.

t: Gemini for healthcare: Google's agent reads Epic, Medicare rules and payer systems for seven launch customers; what to ask before you pilot it
s: Northwell has 400 people fighting insurance denials and wins 90% of them; Google wants both sides of that fight running on its agent. The economics, the safeguards and the questions a health system should put in writing.

t: Gemini Decision 1: 1,000 questions per call, 150 ms, $0.10 per million input tokens and no output bill
s: Google and OpenAI now both sell decisions as a product separate from text; here is what the new API does, where it beats a Flash model, and the three places in an agent loop to try it first.

t: Skild AI's Steel runs robot simulation up to 13x faster than PhysX on mixed batches and uses 62% less memory; here is what the numbers cover
s: A $14 billion startup contributed its rigid-body solver to Nvidia's open-source Newton engine a week after Nvidia shipped Isaac Lab 3.0; the benchmark is real, the headline multiple needs context, and the licence is not stated.

t: Oura pays $625 million for Counsel Health: a 70-person AI primary-care startup is now worth 17 times what it raised
s: A smart-ring maker that could not get its own IPO away is paying up for a chat-first clinic with physicians in the loop; the price says where consumer health AI is heading and what regulators will be watching.

t: Operation Snowball: a jailbroken DeepSeek agent ran a two-week telecom intrusion with a part-time operator, and every exploit was a known CVE
s: Malbear Labs recovered 70 session transcripts from an attacker's open directory; what they show about cost, autonomy and refusal training should change how defenders rank their patch queue.

t: Gemini 4 Carbon is open to every paying developer at $2 / $10 until November 30: what to test before the price doubles
s: Google's strongest model left its cyber-only gate after two weeks, matched Argon's price for 19 days and published safety numbers that are worth reading more closely than the benchmark wins.

t: Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and Meetings: Anthropic now sells an office suite, and here is what IT buyers should ask before the renewal
s: The day before its roadshow, Anthropic turned Claude from a chat window into a workspace with spreadsheets, shared boards, embedded partner apps and a meeting participant; the licence conversation changes with it.

t: Anthropic's IPO range is $70–78: what the amended S-1 says about dilution, lock-ups and the $26 billion partner placement
s: The largest technology listing ever attempted now has a price, a share count and a list of suppliers buying in; here is how to read the numbers before the stock trades.

t: AlphaProof Code verified Signal's protocol code with 6.5 million lines of Lean in four weeks: what AI-written proofs mean for the software you depend on
s: DeepMind's five-person team used agents on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 to prove security properties of libsignal at the machine-code level; the trusted part is the 26,000 lines of spec, and that is where review now belongs.

t: SoftBank's $7 billion loss lands on the day Anthropic starts selling a $1.1–1.3 trillion IPO
s: The largest outside holder of OpenAI just reported its first quarterly loss in two years, and the valuation range for Anthropic's listing has fallen for the third time in a month.

t: Nvidia's GR00T 2 claims 71% one-shot success on 50 tasks. Here is what that number does and does not say
s: A new open world-action model trained on 100,000 hours of human video, a simulator that agents can configure themselves, and a benchmark claim that needs the task list before anyone builds a business case on it.

t: Muse Ember at $0.10 and LongCat-2.5 under MIT: the budget tier is now where agent costs are decided
s: Meta's smallest model matches Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis index at a third of the cost per task, and Meituan has handed developers a 1.6-trillion-parameter model to run themselves.

t: Google's four TPUs in one year: what 8tx and 8i Max mean for anyone negotiating with Nvidia
s: Confidential compute for fine-tuning and a doubled-up inference chip extend the eighth-generation line, and the software around it is now the real competitive move.

t: Fireworks AI's second breach in a month: what inference customers should rotate, review and ask for now
s: An October 24 intrusion through a cloud provider reached billing data, secrets, datasets and partial model weights, weeks after stolen internal credentials exposed customers' stored API keys.

t: Claude Fable 5.2 cuts the top tier to $8 / $40: what actually changes for buyers
s: Anthropic's flagship is 20% cheaper and, on its own numbers, far better at agentic coding, but the company still tells most customers to stay on Opus 5.5.

t: Australia's AI safety regulator: mandatory incident reporting, penalties and model evaluation after the Medicare breach
s: The first Western government to answer a specific AI-agent incident with a statutory regulator has set a template other capitals will copy; the details are still to come.

t: Abridge cuts staff at a $5.3 billion valuation: what it says about the AI scribe market, and what health systems should ask
s: The best-funded company in ambient clinical documentation is flattening its organisation as the category commoditises; buyers mid-contract should get roadmap and support commitments in writing.

t: The PATIENT AI Act draft: a third-party FDA review path and a Medicare pathway, comments due December 1
s: Senator Cassidy's discussion draft is the first serious attempt to legislate how clinical AI gets reviewed and paid for. FDA lawyers say the review title mostly duplicates what the agency can already do.

t: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol discount ends November 30. Here is the price ladder to move to
s: Two vendors' promotional rates expire within a day of each other. OpenAI's pricing page now shows four GPT-6 tiers from $0.10 to $10 per million tokens, and our tracker has caught up.

t: Nvidia's board is investigating Jensen Huang. Here is what is actually at stake
s: An independent review, an admitted affair and a November 18 congressional briefing turn a personal scandal into a governance test for the company the whole AI stack depends on.

t: Inkling 2 Small: a 594B-parameter model trained in 68 hours, priced at $0.30 per million tokens
s: Thinking Machines' second-generation model is a case study in how cheap sparse pretraining has become, and a direct price attack on the mid-tier where closed labs earn their API revenue.

t: Claude Code's 'don't ask again' leaked 2,539 secrets to GitHub. A fix-it checklist
s: The convenience button that stops permission prompts also wrote passwords into a project file that thousands of developers committed. Here is how it happened and what to do today.

t: Anthropic's reported $3.4B generator buy makes power a capital expense for AI labs
s: Taking over 1.7 gigawatts of Caterpillar orders is the biggest known power-equipment purchase by an AI company. It tells you how the labs now think about the grid.

t: Agility Robotics is the first public humanoid company. Its numbers explain why that is hard
s: $174,000 of revenue, a $362 million half-year loss and $300 million of orders for a robot that ships in 2027: AGLT is a bet on throughput targets nobody outside the company has seen. Axon's $1.2 billion Skydio deal shows the other route.

t: Ramp's data says business AI spending has flattened. Here is how to read it
s: A plateau in the share of companies paying for AI tools is not the end of adoption. It is the end of buying everything.

t: Physicl raises $10M to make simulations real enough to train robots, as humanoid funding hits a record
s: The bottleneck in robotics is no longer the model or the hardware. It is believable practice environments, and a new wave of startups is selling exactly that.

t: OpenAI at $1.25T, Anthropic talked down to $1.2–1.3T: the week AI's two giants got repriced
s: Both labs are still worth more than almost any company on earth. What changed is that investors started setting the price instead of accepting it.

t: OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber is rated 'Critical'. Here is what that means for defenders
s: The first model OpenAI has put in its highest cyber-capability tier is gated to vetted customers. The capability itself is not gated anywhere.

t: Gemini 4 Argon's launch price ends November 30. Plan for $4 / $20
s: Google's pricing page now carries an expiry date on its flagship's introductory rate, and the Flash tiers follow in January. Here is the math for anyone who built on launch pricing.

t: After the midterms, the data-center backlash has votes behind it
s: Local measures against new AI data centers won across several states this week. The industry's response, from paying for its own power to warning of slower expansion, tells you how seriously it is taking the result.

t: OpenAI's BioBasicsBench: AI agents score 66.7% on routine lab work, and the failures are the story
s: A new 100-task benchmark tests whether AI can read gels, plates and microscopy like a bench scientist. The headline score is decent; the error cases show why nobody should hand it a pipette yet.

t: AI data-centre economics explained: why a $900 billion compute commitment, a 48% cost of revenue and a '10th percentile' plan all describe the same problem
s: Anthropic's prospectus and its CEO's remarks this week put real numbers on what it costs to run a frontier AI company. Here is how the capital stack works, who carries which risk, and the three questions to ask any vendor or landlord in the chain.

t: What is inference, and why does it cost so much?
s: Training makes a model once; inference runs it every time anyone asks a question. Here is where the money goes, why output tokens cost five times input, and what cached, batch and fast modes actually change.

t: Open-source AI licences explained: Apache 2.0, MIT, Llama-style and 'open-weight' terms, and what each lets you do
s: Inkling 2 Small shipped under Apache 2.0 this week, LongCat-2.5 under MIT, and most 'open' models still ship under something else. Here is what the labels mean, what the patent clause is for, and the three questions to ask before you build on any of them.

t: Open-weight vs closed AI models: what the difference means for you
s: Open-weight models can be downloaded and run anywhere; closed models live behind an API. The trade-offs on cost, control, capability and risk.

t: AI agents: a security checklist for CISOs
s: Agents are software that acts with your credentials. Here are the ten controls that matter, in the order to implement them, with the 2026 incidents that show why each exists.

t: What are non-human identities, and why AI agents make them the biggest hole in your security
s: Service accounts, API keys, OAuth tokens and now agent credentials outnumber people in most companies by ten to one or more. The Railway breach showed what happens when one of them is trusted beyond its job. Here is how to count, scope and kill them.

t: An AI incident response plan: what to do when a model, an agent or an AI vendor goes wrong
s: Breach notices now arrive from inference providers you have never contracted with, agents act faster than on-call rotations, and 'the model did it' is not a root cause. Here is a plan that fits in one page and survives contact with a real incident.

t: LLM API pricing explained: tokens, caching, batch and the cliffs
s: How per-million-token pricing works, why output costs more, and the four levers that cut a bill by half or more.

t: Flagship, mid-tier, small: which AI model tier should you actually use?
s: Every vendor sells three or four sizes. How to match tier to task, and why most production traffic belongs on the middle one.

t: How to read an AI benchmark without being fooled
s: Vendor charts always show the vendor winning. The handful of questions that separate a meaningful result from marketing.

t: Prompt injection explained: the attack every AI agent is exposed to
s: Why text that an AI reads can hijack what it does, why there is no complete fix, and the controls that actually reduce the damage.

t: RAG explained for business leaders
s: Retrieval-augmented generation is how companies make a general model answer from their own documents without retraining it. What it is, what it costs, and where projects fail.

t: What is a context window, and does a million tokens matter?
s: The context window is how much a model can read at once. Why it grew from 4K to 1M tokens, what it costs, and when it actually helps.

t: What is an AI agent? A plain-English explanation
s: An agent is AI that takes actions, not just answers. Here is what that means, why every company is suddenly announcing one, and what can go wrong.

t: Token
s: The unit models read and write; roughly three-quarters of an English word. Pricing and context limits are counted in tokens.

t: Context window
s: The maximum text a model can consider in one request: prompt, documents, conversation and answer combined.

t: Large language model (LLM)
s: A neural network trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next token, which turns out to be enough to write, summarise, reason and code.

t: Agent
s: An AI system that pursues a goal by taking actions with tools, in a loop, rather than answering a single question.

t: Prompt
s: The text sent to a model: instructions, context and the question.

t: System prompt
s: Standing instructions a developer gives a model that apply to every conversation, such as persona, rules and output format.

t: Prompt injection
s: An attack in which text the model reads, such as a web page or email, contains instructions that hijack its behaviour.

t: Jailbreak
s: A user's attempt to make a model ignore its safety rules through crafted prompts.

t: Hallucination
s: A confident, fluent model output that is false or unsupported.

t: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
s: Finding the relevant passages from a document store and giving them to the model with the question, so answers are grounded in your data.

t: Embedding
s: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so similar texts have similar numbers.

t: Vector database
s: A database optimised for storing embeddings and finding the nearest ones to a query.

t: Fine-tuning
s: Further training a model on your own examples to change its behaviour or specialise it.

t: Inference
s: Running a trained model to produce output. What you pay for when you call an API.

t: Training
s: The process of adjusting a model's parameters on data. Pre-training builds general ability; post-training shapes behaviour.

t: Parameters
s: The numbers inside a model that training adjusts; loosely, its size. Frontier models have hundreds of billions to trillions.

t: Weights
s: Another word for a model's parameters, usually in the context of publishing or downloading them.

t: Open-weight model
s: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

t: Closed model
s: A model reachable only through its vendor's API; the weights are not published.

t: Transformer
s: The neural network architecture behind nearly all current language models, built around a mechanism called attention.

t: Attention
s: The mechanism that lets a transformer weigh which earlier tokens matter when producing the next one.

t: Reasoning model
s: A model trained to work through a problem step by step, generating intermediate 'thinking' tokens, before answering.

t: Reasoning budget
s: A setting that controls how many thinking tokens a reasoning model may use before answering.

t: Prompt caching
s: Charging a reduced rate for the repeated prefix of a prompt, such as a system prompt or a document reused across requests.

t: Batch API
s: A way to submit many requests to be processed asynchronously, usually within hours, at about half price.

t: Multimodal
s: A model that accepts or produces more than one kind of input or output: text, images, audio, video.

t: Benchmark
s: A standard test used to compare models, such as a set of coding tasks or exam questions.

t: Evaluation (eval)
s: A test set with known-good answers used to measure a model or system on your own tasks.

t: Guardrails
s: Checks placed around a model to block unwanted inputs or outputs, such as filters for sensitive data or policy violations.

t: Alignment
s: The broad effort to make models behave as their developers and users intend, including being honest and refusing harmful requests.

t: RLHF
s: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model to prefer outputs that human raters rate highly.

t: Tool use (function calling)
s: A model's ability to request that the surrounding software run a function, such as a search or a database query, and return the result.

t: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
s: An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources through a common interface.

t: Latency
s: How long a model takes to respond, usually measured as time to first token and tokens per second.

t: Rate limit
s: The maximum requests or tokens per minute a vendor allows an account, often tiered by spending history.

t: API
s: Application programming interface: the way software calls a model, billed per token, as opposed to a chat app used by a person.

t: Distillation
s: Training a smaller model to imitate a larger one's outputs, capturing much of its capability at lower cost.

t: Mixture of experts (MoE)
s: A model design where only a subset of parameters activates for each token, giving large capacity at lower inference cost.

t: Synthetic data
s: Training data generated by a model rather than collected from humans.

t: Frontier model
s: A model at or near the state of the art at the time, typically the newest top tier from a major lab.

t: Compute
s: The processing power, usually GPU or TPU hours, used to train and run models. The scarce input of the AI industry.

t: GPU
s: Graphics processing unit: the chip type, dominated by Nvidia, that performs the parallel arithmetic AI training and inference require.

t: Non-human identity
s: A credential used by software, including AI agents, rather than a person, such as a service account or API key.

t: Deepfake
s: Synthetic audio, image or video that convincingly impersonates a real person.

t: Grounding
s: Supplying a model with trusted sources (documents, search results) so its answer is tied to evidence rather than memory.

t: Active parameters
s: In a mixture-of-experts model, the subset of parameters actually used for each token. Inkling 2 Small has 594B total but about 17B active.

t: Agent harness
s: The software around a model that turns it into an agent: tool connections, memory, permissions, retries and the loop that decides what to do next.

t: Secret scanning
s: Automated detection of credentials (API keys, passwords, tokens) in code, configuration and history before or after they are committed.

t: 510(k) clearance
s: The FDA pathway that lets a device, including AI software, reach market by showing it is substantially equivalent to an already-authorised predicate device.

t: Staged release
s: Publishing a model's weights only after a sequence of gated steps, typically API access, external safety testing and red-teaming, rather than on launch day.

t: Prefill and decode
s: The two phases of inference: reading the whole prompt in one parallel pass (prefill), then generating the answer one token at a time (decode).

t: Confidential computing
s: Hardware that keeps data and model weights encrypted and isolated while they are being processed, not only at rest or in transit.

t: World action model
s: A robot foundation model that predicts how the world will change and chooses actions from that prediction, rather than mapping images straight to motor commands.

t: LLMjacking
s: Stealing API keys or cloud credentials to run large language models at someone else's expense, or to resell that access.

t: Cost per task
s: What it costs to get a job completed by a model, including hidden reasoning tokens, retries and tool calls, as opposed to the list price per token.

t: Formal verification
s: Mathematically proving that software or hardware satisfies a precise specification, usually with a proof assistant such as Lean that checks every step.

t: Sub-processor
s: A vendor's own vendor that handles your data on its behalf, such as the inference provider behind a SaaS product's AI feature.

t: Lock-up period
s: The window after an IPO during which insiders and pre-IPO investors are barred from selling shares, typically 180 days.

t: Physics engine (robot simulation)
s: Software that simulates rigid bodies, contact and friction so robot control policies can be trained on millions of virtual trials before touching hardware.

t: Decision model
s: A model that scores a fixed set of options and returns probabilities instead of generating text, used for routing, tool selection, policy checks and grading.

t: Spend cap (API)
s: A hard monthly or daily limit on what an API key can charge, set at the provider, after which requests fail.

t: Frontier AI framework
s: The published safety policy a large frontier developer must maintain under New York's RAISE Act and California's SB 53, describing how it assesses and mitigates catastrophic risk.

t: Adjusted operating loss
s: A company's operating loss after excluding items it chooses to leave out, typically stock compensation and one-off charges; not a GAAP measure.

t: Sandbox escape
s: Breaking out of the isolation that is supposed to keep one tenant's code, or one agent's actions, from reaching the host or other tenants.

t: NVFP4
s: Nvidia's 4-bit floating-point weight format, used to train and serve very large models on Blackwell-class GPUs with roughly a quarter of the memory of 16-bit weights.

t: Expert parallelism
s: Splitting a mixture-of-experts model across GPUs by expert rather than by layer, so each GPU holds a subset of the experts and tokens are routed to the right device.

t: Thinking level
s: A vendor setting that controls how much reasoning a model does before answering, trading latency and tokens for accuracy; Google's Gemini 4 models offer low, medium, high and xhigh.

t: Public nuisance (AI litigation)
s: A tort claim that conduct harms the public's health, safety or shared rights; historically used against pollution and opioids, now pleaded against frontier AI development.

t: Webshell
s: A small script an attacker uploads to a web server so they can run commands on it through a browser; the classic first foothold in a server intrusion.

t: Network token (payments)
s: A substitute card number issued by Visa, Mastercard or American Express for one transaction or merchant, so the real card details never reach the merchant or the software making the purchase.

t: Semantic versioning
s: A version-number convention (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) in which breaking changes bump the first number, compatible additions the second and bug fixes the third.

t: Spot compute
s: Accelerator capacity bought on short notice at the going rate rather than reserved years ahead under contract.

t: Reserved special token
s: A vocabulary entry a model's tokeniser treats as a control symbol rather than text, so no user or document content can produce it.

t: Indirect prompt injection
s: An attack in which malicious instructions are hidden in content the model reads (a web page, email, document or tool result) rather than typed by the user.
